definition.text: A refinement of Nash equilibrium for games with moves in sequence, requiring the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward.

facts.text: It rules out non-credible threats, so strategies stay rational throughout the game.
Reinhard Selten proposed it in 1965.
Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall has one.
In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite or imperfect-information games.
The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria.
In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round.
Firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium if they are patient enough.

title: Backward induction

definition.text: Solving a sequential game by starting from the last move, working out what the final mover would do, and reasoning back to the start.

facts.text: At each step it removes branches where a player would make a move that is not in their interest at that point.
Tic-tac-toe has a well-known backward-induction solution, and in theory even Go has one.
Finite repeated games can be solved this way, but games repeated forever or an unknown number of times cannot, as there is no last round.
Kaminski (2019) proved that a generalized backward induction finds all subgame perfect equilibria in a broad class of games.

title: Credible threat

definition.text: A threat a player would actually want to carry out if the time came; a non-credible threat is one that would hurt the player making it.

facts.text: Plain Nash equilibrium can rest on threats players would never carry out; subgame perfection eliminates them.
In Chicken, a player who rips out their steering wheel always wins, because the opponent's threat to crash anyway is not credible.
If punishing a deviator is costly to the punishers, the threat of punishment is not credible.

notes: No page of its own; discussed on Subgame perfect equilibrium, Nash equilibrium, Folk theorem and Cooperative game theory.

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates on the first move and then copies whatever the opponent did on the previous move.

facts.text: The phrase means 'equivalent retaliation' and was first recorded in 1558.
Anatol Rapoport entered it in Robert Axelrod's two tournaments around 1980, where it was both the simplest strategy and the most successful.
Its success may help explain how animal and human groups came to live in mostly cooperative ways.
A single misread move can trap two tit-for-tat players in an endless 'death spiral' of alternating retaliation.
It is not a subgame perfect equilibrium except under knife-edge conditions on the discount rate.
In First World War trenches it appeared as the 'live and let live' system, an unspoken truce kept by matching retaliation.
In repeated social dilemmas, cooperation may emerge when people adopt tit for tat.

title: Tit for two tats
article: Tit for tat#Tit for two tats

definition.text: A more forgiving version of tit for tat that retaliates only after the opponent defects twice in a row.

facts.text: Letting a single defection pass avoids the 'death spiral' of two retaliators punishing each other forever.
Robert Axelrod found it would have outscored every program in his first tournament.
BitTorrent file-sharing peers use a variant of it to swap upload for download bandwidth.

title: Generous tit for tat
article: Tit for tat#Generous tit for tat

definition.text: A version of tit for tat that, after the opponent defects, usually retaliates but sometimes cooperates anyway, with a small probability.

facts.text: Occasional forgiveness breaks cycles of retaliation caused by mistakes or 'noise' and restores mutual cooperation.
Axelrod found it highly effective in noisy settings; the forgiveness probability can be around 1–5%, depending on the opponents.

title: Reciprocal altruism
article: Tit for tat#Explaining reciprocal altruism in animal communities

definition.text: Helping another animal in the expectation that the favour will be returned when needs reverse, explained by tit-for-tat strategies.

facts.text: It works where the cost to the helper of sharing food, mates, nests or territory is less than the gain to the one helped.
Ways of spotting and punishing 'cheaters' who fail to return favours, in effect tit for tat, keep it stable.
Tit for tat has been suggested as the mechanism behind guppies' cooperative inspection of predators.

title: Axelrod's tournaments
article: Prisoner's dilemma#Axelrod's tournament and successful strategy conditions

definition.text: Computer tournaments organized by Robert Axelrod in which strategies submitted by academics competed in the repeated prisoner's dilemma.

facts.text: Greedy strategies did poorly over the long run, and the simple tit for tat won.
Axelrod concluded that successful strategies are nice, retaliating, forgiving and non-envious.
He used the results to show how altruism could evolve by natural selection from purely selfish beginnings, reported in his 1984 book The Evolution of Cooperation.
